title: Fermat, Euler, and modular powers
terms: Fermat little theorem; Euler totient function; Euler theorem; modular exponentiation.

Reduce an exponent modulo a known period only after checking that the base is invertible.
Repeated squaring computes powers even when no theorem applies. A number satisfying a
Fermat congruence need not be prime, and the order of an individual unit can be much smaller
than φ(n).

question.text:
222
What is the remainder of 7 on division by 13?
(A) 1 (B) 3 (C) 5 (D) 8 (E) 12

solution.text:
2 3 6
Fermat reduces 222 modulo 12 to 6. Since 7 ≡ 10, 7 ≡ 5, and 7 ≡ 25 ≡ 12 (mod 13), the
remainder is 12.

question.text:
1000
What is the remainder of 3 on division by 40?
(A) 1 (B) 3 (C) 9 (D) 21 (E) 27

solution.text:
4
The base is coprime to 40. More directly than Euler, 3 = 81 ≡ 1 (mod 40). Since 4 | 1000,
the required remainder is 1.

question.text:
96
How many residue classes a modulo 360 satisfy a ≡ 1 (mod 360)?
(A) 48 (B) 72 (C) 96 (D) 120 (E) 360

solution.text:
The totient is 360(1 − 1/2)(1 − 1/3)(1 − 1/5) = 96, so every unit satisfies the congruence
by Euler. A nonunit shares a prime factor with 360; reducing modulo that prime makes the
left side zero and the right side one, impossible. Thus exactly the ninety-six units work.

question.text:
120
What is the remainder of 2 on division by 72?
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 8 (D) 16 (E) 64

solution.text:
6
Modulo eight the power is zero. Modulo nine, Euler gives 2 ≡ 1, so the power is one.
Among multiples of eight below seventy-two, only sixty-four is one modulo nine. Reduc-
ing 120 modulo φ(72) = 24 directly would be invalid because two is not a unit modulo
seventy-two.

question.text:
10
Since 2 = 1024 = 3 · 341 + 1, which statement is correct?
(A) 341 must be prime.
340
(B) 2 ̸≡ 1 (mod 341).
340
(C) 2 ≡ 1 (mod 341) although 341 is composite.
(D) The order of 2 modulo 341 is 340.
(E) Fermat's little theorem is false.

solution.text:
340
Raising the given congruence to the thirty-fourth power gives 2 ≡ 1. But 341 =
11 · 31 is composite. A Fermat congruence for one base is a necessary condition for primality
in the usual coprime setting, not a sufficient condition. Here the order divides ten.
